newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Beef battles to occupy Irish EU farm campaign.
newsitem.headline: Beef battles to occupy Irish EU farm campaign.

text.p: The stage is set for more beef battles during the rest of the Irish EU Presidency as Britain fights to end a worldwide ban on its beef exports and farm ministers argue over steps to aid the market and restore consumer confidence.

As a major beef producer and exporter, Ireland will make every effort to calm the crisis which cut European Union beef demand by an average 11 percent and intervention stocks forecast to rise to 650,000 tonnes, from zero, by end-1996.

British Prime Minister John Major has set a November deadline for lifting the ban imposed by the European Commission on March 27 after London triggered a public health scare by saying that mad cow disease could be transmitted to humans.

EU officials said that the British deadline was unrealistic, especially after London announced on August 1 that a new study showed that the disease, known medically as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be passed to calves.4
The study implied that more cattle would have to be culled, something British farmers strongly oppose, and raised doubts about the safety of milk.
Independent EU veterinary scientists, who met last Friday, decided to study the two issues further.
A multi-disciplinary committee, bringing together animal, public health, food, cosmetics and other scientific experts, will also discuss the issues on September 16.
Farm ministers, who meet on the same day for the first time following the summer break, are due to discuss Commission beef reform proposals (COM(96)422) designed to deal with the mad cow crisis.
The proposals amend three regulations:
a) (REG(68)805) on the beef common market organisation.
b) (REG(92)1765) on the arable crops support system.
c) (REG(91)2328) on structural aids
But a decision will only be possible at their next meeting on October 28-29 after the European Parliament last week refused to give an opinion saying that it needed more time.
The European Commission proposed on July 30 a series of measures to reduce beef production to help avoid a build-up of surpluses as consumers shun beef due to the mad cow crisis.

Young male cattle of between seven and nine months would be eligible for intervention storage, 1996 and 1997 intervention tonnage ceilings raised and ceilings on the number of male cattle receiving the special beef premium reduced.
A calf slaughter scheme in Britain and Portugal would be extended to all member states and greater incentives offered for extensive beef production.

The package, which would cost 1.3 billion Ecus ($1.7 billion) in 1997, would be financed by a reduction in compensation payments to cereals farmers for income losses due to 1992 production-cutting reforms.
The beef reforms and financing plans have already been fiercely criticised by Germany which says its farmers would suffer disproportionately and that funds could be found elsewhere in the budget.

Austria, France and other member states have also criticised the proposals which look set for a rough ride with possibly only immediate impact measures, notably intervention limits and eligibility, likely to be approved in October.
Beef promotion will be the theme of an informal meeting of farm ministers in Killarney, Ireland, from September 22-24.
As a major beef exporter, Ireland is particularly anxious to restore beef demand which has fallen by up to thirty percent in countries such as Italy and Germany.
Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler is expected to outline plans for an EU beef labelling scheme as a formal proposal is unlikely to be ready in time.
The labelling scheme, which is aimed at boosting consumer confidence, would show the origin of the meat and how it was produced. Austria, Belgium and the Netherlands already have national schemes.
Other issues to be dealt with in the remaining Irish presidency are:
- SHEEPMEAT AND BSE: EU veterinary scientists recommended on Friday that protective measures should be taken according to the risks in each country.
It was a rebuff for Fischler who in July sought EU-wide measures after reports from Britain and France that sheep could catch BSE under laboratory conditions.
Fischler had proposed banning suspect tissues such as sheep brains, spleens and spinal cords from the human and animal food chains to protect human health.
But this was strongly opposed by countries where no BSE cases had been reported.

- SHEEPMEAT REFORM: Some member states, notably Ireland, say that the ewe premium, which compensates farmers for the difference between the EU basic price and the average marketing price, is insufficient.

- VEAL CRATES: Little progress is expected on this dossier due to the mad cow crisis. The Commission proposed on January 24 (COM 96 21) to ban all veal crates for rearing calves from 2008. New or renovated crates would be banned from 1988 and old crates phased out over 10 years. French, Italian, Dutch and Belgian farmers, the main users of veal crates, have protested that the proposal would ruin them.

- WINE REFORM: Little progress is expected on proposals to remove wine surpluses and improve quality (COM(94)117). The proposals have been held up by strong opposition from southern producer countries which said quota cuts were too great abd compensation too little. The outgoing Italian EU Presidency asked the Commission to revise its proposal because the surpluses had disappeared. Fischler said the Commission would study whether the improved market situation was due to structural or cyclical facrtors, notably poor weather.

- OLIVE OIL REFORM: The Commission plans to present a long expected reform proposal on October 9. In the producer camp, Italy wants aid linked to the olive tree area or number of trees. But Spain wants a production-linked aid system combined for large and small producers. Consumer countries are mostly concerned about limiting costs and curbing fraud.
- TOBACCO REFORM: The Commission plans to issue a report later this year on the tobacco market, putting forward suggested changes.

- RURAL DEVELOPMENT: A conference, to be held in Cork on November 7-9, is expected to lay the basis for future farm reforms making the environment a central element of farm policy. Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler and Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates will be among the speakers.

- MEAT HORMONES: A World Trade Organisation disputes panel is due to meet in Geneva on October 10 to hear Washington's complaint against the EU's ban on imports of beef treated with growth hormones. The United States, along with Australia, New Zealand and Canada, say that the meat is safe and that the ban is not scientifically justified. But Fischler has said that consumer concerns must be safeguarded. The WTO panel is not expected to reach any conclusion until at least mid-1997.
- BANANAS: A WTO disputes panel met for the first time on September 10 to hear a complaint from the United States that EU banana import quotas favour Caribbean producers and breach free trade rules.

Meanwhile a Commission proposal (COM(95)115) to increase the import quota for "dollar" bananas by 353,000 tonnes to 2.53 million tonnes to cater for new members Austria, Sweden and Finland remains blocked. So is a proposal (COM(95)114) to exclude small fig bananas from the banana regime (EEC404/93). Germany, backed by the new members, opposes the proposals unless the EU imports more cheaper "dollar" bananas from Latin America.

- WORLD FOOD SUMMIT: In Rome Nov 13-17, the EU will be under pressure from developing countries, who have been squeezed by record grain prices over the past year, to guarantee adequate supplies at affordable prices.

- EAST EUROPE: No date has been set for a meeting between EU farm ministers and their counterparts from 10 applicant countries in central and eastern Europe. The Commission's DG VI for agriculture is currently evaluating replies from the applicant countries to a questionaire aimed at assessing their state of readiness.

- VETERINARY AND PHYTOSANITARY: The Commission is aiming to conclude agreements with the United States, Canada, Argentina, Uruguay, Australia, New Zealand and several eastern European countries by the end of 1996. The accords will allow mutual recognition of animal and plant health standards and ease trade in live animals, fresh and processed meat, plants, plant products, pet food and other catefgories.
Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates has said he wants to make progress on consolidating the much amended Directive(64)432 on trade between member states in cattle and pigs.
- MOUNTAIN AGRICULTURE: Austria and Italy are expected to press for a follow-up to memorandums submitted in July 1996 and February 1995 requesting changes in aid schemes for mountain farmers.

- FOOD LAW: A long expected joint discussion paper with the industry and consumer services on ways to simplify rules on food safety, hygiene and labelling, may eventually surface. The paper has been held up by squabbling between the services.
- YOUNG FARMERS: Ministers are due to discuss a Commission report (COM(96)398), issued on September 6, on ways to help young farmers start-up and rejuvenate an ageing farming population.

- FREE TRADE ACCORDS: A follow-up is expected to discussions at an informal farm ministers' meeting in Otranto, Italy, about concerns that EU free trade pacts with east European, latin American and other developing countries were harming its farmers, especially in southern member states.
